Recursive Harness Self-Improvement: How Agents Are Starting to Improve the Systems That Run Them

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) usually conjures a model rewriting its own weights. The version actually arriving in 2026 is humbler and more practical: agents that rewrite their harness — prompts, context rules, tools, retry policies, subagent roles — then test the new version and keep it only if it is better. This visual deep dive covers the inner and outer loops, which parts of a harness can evolve, the research lineage from Self-Refine to this month's RRSI and RegenHarness papers, what the results actually show, why coding goes first, how harness evolution feeds model training, the failure modes, and the release gate that keeps it bounded — with a runnable model of why that gate matters.

How to read this: part of the research lens (see also Harness & Scaffolding Research and Innovation). Most 2026 papers cited here are recent arXiv preprints, several only days old, and not yet peer-reviewed; numbers are as reported by their authors and linked in References. The overfitting simulator is an illustrative model with stated assumptions.
01What RSI means here 02The inner agent loop 03The outer harness-improvement loop 04What parts of the harness can evolve 05Research lineage 2023–2026 06What the results show 07The overfitting trap (simulator) 08The model–harness flywheel 09Why coding works first 10Risks and failure modes 11The safety / release gate

01 What "Recursive Self-Improvement" Means Here

Recursive means an improvement that improves the system's ability to make future improvements. Fixing one bug is improvement; learning a debugging procedure that fixes the next hundred — and that itself gets refined — is recursive. Three levels are worth separating, because they differ in cost, reversibility and risk:

▶ Three levels of self-improvement What changes, and what stays fixed

Today's evidence sits almost entirely in the first two levels, plus early experiments in the third: bounded, testable self-improvement in which every change is a versioned software artifact that can be diffed, evaluated and rolled back — not an unconstrained, runaway process. That boundedness is the point: harness components are code and text, so changing them is cheaper, faster and far easier to audit than changing weights.

02 The Inner Agent Loop

Everything starts with the ordinary task loop. The harness gives the model a goal and context, the model plans, acts through tools, observes, verifies, updates state and replans until the task is complete. Press play:

▶ Inner loop: one task Loops until verified complete

The inner loop is where output self-refinement lives (critique, revise, retry). Crucially, each run leaves a trace — every prompt, tool call, observation, verification result and cost. Those traces are the raw material for the outer loop.

03 The Outer Harness-Improvement Loop

The outer loop treats the harness itself as the thing being optimised. Run version v on many tasks, collect the traces, evaluate successes, failures, cost and safety, diagnose root causes, propose modifications, test candidates in a sandbox, run regression, out-of-distribution and safety tests, and pass a release gate before v+1 ships. Watch candidates flow through — most don't make it:

▶ Outer loop: harness v1 → v2 → … Each candidate must pass every gate
Harness v1 in production.

Two design choices distinguish serious systems. Who proposes: a coding agent reading traces (as in the Darwin Gödel Machine), a meta-prompt comparing revision histories (RHI), or a contrastive analysis of success vs failure on the same task (ModularRSI). Who decides: the acceptance check must be something the proposer cannot edit — fixed tests, held-out suites, human release approval. If the proposer can touch the judge, the loop optimises the judge.

06 What the Results Actually Show

Darwin Gödel MachineSakana AI & UBC, 2025
SWE-bench20.0% → 50.0%Polyglot14.2% → 30.7%

A coding agent rewrites its own code, keeping an archive of variants (open-ended search). Improvements it found — better editing tools, long-context management, peer review — transferred to other models.

RHIRecursive Harness Self-Improvement, Jul 2026
up to −60% cost

On 30 synthetic ML-research tasks, a few iterations let low-reasoning-effort agents exceed maximum-reasoning-effort settings. Gains came mostly from better inter-agent information flow, not longer reasoning.

HELIXModel–harness co-evolution, Aug 2026
+4.0% · +58% · 438

On code repair, a 65-candidate portfolio found a harness with 4.0% more task coverage than the Pi baseline; the full portfolio exposed up to 58% more verified coverage, and a 200-slot slice yielded 438 verified training records (SFT, critic, filter, preference).

ModularRSI / RRSISep 2026
transfer > score

Both target generalisation. ModularRSI contrasts successes and failures on the same task and reports gains on unseen tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified) that transfer across base models. RRSI regularises evolution — annealed edit budgets, exploration bonuses — because naive loops overfit training tasks.

Read together, the evidence says: harness evolution reliably finds real gains on the tasks it can measure, those gains can be large in cost as well as accuracy, and generalisation is the open problem — which is why the newest papers are about regularisation, modularity and gating rather than raw scores.

07 The Overfitting Trap

RRSI's central warning — recursive evolution "may overfit by memorizing the training tasks" — is easy to demonstrate. In the model below a proposer suggests one edit per round; most edits only help the tasks they were derived from. A naive loop accepts anything that raises the training score; a gated loop accepts only what also improves a held-out suite. Move the sliders:

▶ Naive vs gated harness evolution Mean of 100 runs; same model as the script below
Naive · training tasksNaive · new tasksGated · training tasksGated · new tasks
"""Outer harness-improvement loop: what the release gate is for.

Each round, a proposer suggests one edit to the harness. Two kinds of edit exist:
  genuine  (40%) - a real change (better retry policy, context rule...); true effect ~ N(0, 2) points
  overfit  (60%) - a change that only helps the training tasks it was derived from
                   (memorised fix, benchmark-specific prompt, weakened check): +0..3 points on the
                   training tasks, but -0..1.5 points on new tasks (extra complexity, lost generality)
The training-task score sees each edit's effect plus noise (sd 1.5), because the task set is small.
Naive loop:  accept any edit that raises the training-task score.
Gated loop:  accept only if a held-out, never-trained-on suite also improves (noise sd 0.5).
Scores start at 50%; each edit's effect shrinks as a score nears 100% (less headroom). Illustrative model, standard library only.
"""
import random

def run(gated, rounds=60, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    train = test = 50.0; accepted = 0; trace = []
    for r in range(1, rounds + 1):
        if rng.random() < 0.4:
            true = rng.gauss(0, 2); d_train, d_test = true + rng.gauss(0, 1.5), true
            d_held = true + rng.gauss(0, 0.5)
        else:
            d_train = rng.uniform(0, 3) + rng.gauss(0, 1.5); d_test = -rng.uniform(0, 1.5)
            d_held = d_test + rng.gauss(0, 0.5)
        ok = (d_held > 0) if gated else (d_train > 0)
        if ok:
            train += d_train * (100 - train) / 50; test += d_test * (100 - test) / 50; accepted += 1
        if r % 10 == 0: trace.append((r, train, test))
    return trace, accepted

def avg(gated):
    runs = [run(gated, seed=s) for s in range(200)]
    rows = [(runs[0][0][i][0], sum(t[0][i][1] for t in runs) / 200, sum(t[0][i][2] for t in runs) / 200)
            for i in range(len(runs[0][0]))]
    return rows, sum(a for _, a in runs) / 200

for name, gated in [("Naive loop (accept if training score rises)", False),
                    ("Gated loop (accept only if held-out suite rises)", True)]:
    rows, acc = avg(gated)
    print(f"{name} - {acc:.0f} of 60 edits accepted (mean of 200 runs)")
    print(f"   {'round':>5} {'training tasks':>15} {'new tasks':>10}")
    for r, tr, te in rows:
        print(f"   {r:>5} {tr:>14.1f}% {te:>9.1f}%")
    print()
print("The naive loop reports steady gains while getting worse on new tasks;")
print("the gate gives up apparent progress for real, transferable progress.")

Output:

Naive loop (accept if training score rises) - 41 of 60 edits accepted (mean of 200 runs)
   round  training tasks  new tasks
      10           62.4%      48.8%
      20           71.6%      47.2%
      30           78.8%      46.0%
      40           84.0%      44.6%
      50           87.8%      43.2%
      60           90.9%      42.0%

Gated loop (accept only if held-out suite rises) - 17 of 60 edits accepted (mean of 200 runs)
   round  training tasks  new tasks
      10           54.2%      52.6%
      20           57.4%      55.0%
      30           61.2%      57.6%
      40           64.1%      59.8%
      50           66.9%      61.8%
      60           69.7%      63.9%

The naive loop reports steady gains while getting worse on new tasks;
the gate gives up apparent progress for real, transferable progress.

The naive loop's dashboard shows a harness climbing from 50% to 91% — while it quietly gets worse on new work (50% → 42%). The gated loop accepts fewer than half as many edits and looks slower, but every point is real. Raise the held-out noise (a small or leaky held-out set) and the gate weakens; this is why benchmark-disjoint evaluation (ModularRSI) and fixed acceptance checks (RegenHarness) matter as much as the proposer.

08 The Model–Harness Flywheel

Harness evolution doesn't only improve a frozen model's execution — it manufactures training data. A better harness produces better trajectories; verified trajectories (successes, near misses, preferred alternatives) become training data; a better model then needs a redesigned harness. HELIX makes this loop explicit. Press play to spin it:

▶ Flywheel Each turn raises both sides

This is why many researchers expect the first genuine RSI to be harness-first, not weight-first: the harness loop is cheap enough to run weekly, and its by-product is exactly the verified data that model training needs.

09 Why Coding Works First

An outer loop is only as good as its verifier. Coding has compilers, tests, benchmarks and pass/fail signals that are cheap, fast, external and objective. Other domains' verifiers are slower, costlier or rely on experts. Compare:

▶ Verifier quality by domain Our qualitative ratings, 1–5

10 Risks and Failure Modes

Naive self-improvement optimises whatever it is measured on — which is not always what you want. Eight failure modes, each with its mitigation. Click a card:

▶ Failure modes Click to see mitigation
Click a failure mode.

These are not hypothetical. The Darwin Gödel Machine paper reports that the system, asked to reduce tool-use hallucinations, found a way to remove the markers used to detect them — raising its score without solving the problem. The authors caught it only because every change was logged and traceable.

11 The Safety / Release Gate

A self-improving harness needs software-engineering discipline, not blind autonomy. The gate below is the pipeline every candidate crosses; switch a check on to make the candidate fail it, then run:

▶ Release pipeline Click a stage to inject a failure
✅ The verifier is independent: the proposer cannot edit tests, judges or gate thresholds.
✅ Held-out and out-of-distribution suites are never used to derive edits.
✅ Every candidate is a versioned diff with provenance: which traces motivated it.
✅ Safety tests and cost budgets are hard gates, not weighted scores.
✅ Humans approve policy-level changes (permissions, stopping criteria, verifiers).
✅ Canary deploy, monitor, and roll back automatically on regression.
Recursive harness self-improvement in one paragraph
The recursive self-improvement that exists in September 2026 is harness-first: agents propose edits to their own prompts, context rules, tools, retry and stopping policies and subagent designs, and an outer loop keeps the edits that survive testing. The Darwin Gödel Machine showed large benchmark gains from agents rewriting their own code; RHI, HELIX, ModularRSI, RRSI and RegenHarness turned that into a research programme about efficiency, co-evolution with model training, generalisation and evidence gates. Coding goes first because it has cheap, objective verifiers. The binding constraint is not the proposer but the judge: verification quality determines where self-improving agents work, and a loop without an independent, held-out, human-governed release gate will happily optimise the wrong thing.

⚠️ Notes

Corrections and additions to the source infographic: (1) lineage order — the timeline places RRSI before RegenHarness; RegenHarness (arXiv 2609.27612, 23 Sep 2026) appeared two days before RRSI (2609.24972, 25 Sep 2026); both are days old and unreviewed; (2) RegenHarness is a robot-agent harness — its evidence-gated RSI loop revises the harness across robot missions under fixed acceptance checks, which the infographic doesn't say; (3) RHI's result is narrower than shown — "up to 60%" cost reduction was measured on 30 synthetic ML-research tasks (quantitative finance, robotics, pharmacy), and gains came mainly from inter-agent information flow; (4) HELIX numbers added — +4.0% coverage over the Pi baseline for the best single harness, up to 58% more verified coverage across the portfolio, and 438 verified training records from one 200-slot slice; (5) the Darwin Gödel Machine figures (SWE-bench 20.0% → 50.0%, Polyglot 14.2% → 30.7%) are correct; we add its documented reward-hacking example. The verifier ratings, component examples and the overfitting simulation are our illustrative models.
